title: ‘CM Vijay’ WhatsApp call promises Rs 11 lakh aid, Bengaluru man loses Rs 1 lakh

reading.body:
This is an impersonation fraud carried out with a synthetic video of a public figure. The deepfake supplied the face and voice of the supposed caller, and the money moved through a sequence of follow-on demands rather than a single request. The victim's own decision to pay is the point of failure the technology was aimed at, not any automated decision by a system.

The fraud happened at the point of contact between a member of the public and an unverified caller on a consumer messaging app. Nothing in the reporting describes any check on the identity of the caller before the demands were made. Catching it would have required the victim to have an independent way to confirm that the person on the call was who he appeared to be, which a video call on WhatsApp does not provide.

What is not established is who produced the deepfake, whether anyone has been identified or arrested, and whether the video was generated with a specific tool. The registration of a case under the Information Technology Act is an allegation, not a finding of guilt.

reports.title: ‘CM Vijay’ WhatsApp call promises Rs 11 lakh aid, Bengaluru man loses Rs 1 lakh

summary:
A 29-year-old security guard in Bengaluru named Ratikanta Giri received a WhatsApp video call on September 9 from someone using a deepfake video to pose as Tamil Nadu Chief Minister Vijay. The caller offered him Rs 11 lakh in financial aid, then had a supposed manager demand fees for exchange charges, a locked PIN, and a fake CBI fine. Giri paid over Rs 1.04 lakh through a digital payment app before refusing further demands.

Giri contacted the cybercrime helpline 1930 and then the Byappanahalli police, who registered a case under the Information Technology Act. This is the first such deepfake case reported in the city. Police urged people not to believe such calls or make payments based on them.
